newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FUND VIEW - Thai float the right step in a long haul. [CORRECTED 10:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Thai float the right step in a long haul. [CORRECTED 10:40 GMT]

text.p: Thailand's effective devaluation of its currency on Wednesday was the right step on its long road to economic recovery and should give a much-needed boost to its beleagured stock market, fund managers said.

But they cautioned that the move was far from a cure-all for a country beset by a variety of political and financial woes and noted long-term investment decisions would still be based on how the troubled economy responded to the medicine.

Many funds have already been nibbling at Thai stocks. And while the baht nose-dived on foreign exchange markets, the prospects of still cheaper prices lured foreign institutions to the stock market on a buying spree.
By midday, the key SET index had soared 40.93 points, or 7.76 percent, to 568.21, with many stocks rising to the 10 percent daily limit.
"This is what people have been waiting for. It's a step in the right direction, but not the end of their worries," said Hugh Young, director of Abtrust Fund Managers (Singapore) Ltd.
He said Abtrust had been buying Thai stocks before the news broke because the stocks were cheap. However, "They still face a long haul," he added.
Thailand's central bank announced on Wednesday that its currency would be governed by a managed flotation and would no longer be set against a basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar.

It also raised its key lending rate two percentage points to 12.5 percent to prevent the currency from going into a freefall. Currency analysts said it remained unclear what level the central bank was seeking for the baht, although they anticipated a 15 percent devaluation to around 30.00 to the U.S. dollar.
The move stunned the Thai foreign exchange markets and sent ripples through other regional markets.
The frail Thai currency dropped sharply in offshore markets to 27.00/28.00 to the dollar from 24.35 when the announcement was made.
Central banks in Malaysia (corrects from Indonesia) and the Philippines rallied to defend their currencies which suffered from the fall in the baht.

Many fund managers had predicted a devaluation, but had expected the government would wait until the market turmoil had calmed and it saw some flicker of improvement in the economy. "This (the Thai flotation) was a surprise. I thought they would have waited until they saw some improvement in the economy," said one fund manager who asked not to be named.
"We still have to see how long it will take for there to be an improvement in the economy...If interest rates stay high for too long, it will defeat the purpose of the devaluation."
Until the picture becomes clearer, he said he would maintain his neutral weighting.
Some fund managers said Thailand's stock index, which has been hovering at eight-year lows recently, would rally to the 650 or 700 level.
"I think we will see that reached fairly quickly, but then it could become volatile," Sriyan Pietersz, chief strategist at Capital Nomura Securities told Reuters Financial Television.
"After that, we will look at the BOT's (Bank of Thailand's) interest rate policy and what impact they can expect on the economy and the corporate sector," he added.
